title: Modern Hitmakers Top First-Ever Ranking of Country Music’s Greatest Songwriters
summary: Quick: name the most successful country songwriter in history. If you guessed Willie Nelson or Kris Kristofferson, you’d be wrong — at least according to a groundbreaking new study. Record Research, the company behind the famed “Whitburn books,” has crunched 81 years of Billboard country charts to produce the first-ever ranking of the genre’s top songwriters. The results might surprise you. Sitting at No. 1 is Ashley Gorley, the pen behind recent smashes like “I Had Some Help” and “I Am Not Okay.” Right behind him at No. 2 is Shane McAnally, known for “Body Like a Back Road” and “Mama’s Broken Heart.” Both have been churning out hits for over 15 years, but they also benefit from the modern era: the study weights Billboard’s Country Airplay chart more heavily than the streaming-influenced Hot Country Songs, yet the latter still allows songs to rack up points quickly when they go viral. “Because of the impact of streaming services, there tends to be less curation,” explains Record Research partner Vinnie Freda. “The consumer has a little bit more of a say.” That democratization has helped prolific contemporary writers climb the ranks. The top 10 is a mix of behind-the-scenes craftsmen and a few artist-writers. Bill Anderson (No. 4) and Merle Haggard (No. 10) are the only two who were also performers throughout their careers. Bob McDill (No. 3), who wrote “Gone Country,” and Rhett Akins (No. 9) both started out wanting to be artists but found their true calling in writing. Rounding out the list are Harlan Howard (No. 5), Billy Sherrill (No. 6), Craig Wiseman (No. 7), and Tom Shapiro (No. 8). The full top 40 appears in the new book Top Country Singles 1944-2025, published June 4 to coincide with CMA Fest in Nashville. Freda, who revived Record Research after founder Joel Whitburn’s death, says the project was inspired by a desire to honor songwriters as “unsung heroes.” He also sees charts as cultural memory banks. “A song that spends 10 weeks on a chart tends to be more in the collective memory of our society than a song that spent one week at 34,” he says. For country fans, the list is a treasure map of the songs that have shaped their lives — even if they never knew who wrote them.
why_it_matters: This ranking pulls back the curtain on who actually creates the songs that become the soundtrack of millions of lives, revealing that the music industry often hides the people behind the hits — and it challenges us to think about how chart rules shape whose work gets remembered.

background_read: Record Research is a company famous for its 'Whitburn books,' founded by Joel Whitburn (1939–2022), who obsessively compiled Billboard chart data into reference books used by music historians and fans.
The Billboard charts began in 1940, and the country music charts have tracked radio airplay, sales, and now streaming across 81 years, measuring a song's commercial impact.
CMA Fest in Nashville is one of the largest country music festivals in the world, held annually since 1972, where thousands of fans and artists gather for performances and industry events.

Ashley Gorley has written over 60 No. 1 country hits for stars like Luke Bryan and Morgan Wallen; Shane McAnally has penned hits for Sam Hunt and Miranda Lambert, often bringing modern pop influences into country.
Many iconic country songs were written by people who never became famous performers themselves — like Bob McDill, who wrote 'Gone Country' but stayed behind the scenes.

perspectives.description: For decades, songwriters were often invisible to the public while their songs made stars; this ranking gives them credit and might lead listeners to appreciate the craft behind the hooks.

Heavy weighting of the Country Airplay chart favors songs that radio programmers chose, potentially underrepresenting older eras where streaming didn't exist, raising questions about how 'fair' cross-era rankings can ever be.
Chart-based rankings always reflect the technology and consumption habits of their time; this study parallels baseball sabermetrics, where new weighting methods recast who we consider 'the greatest.'

As streaming services continue to influence listening, future rankings may include more granular data about songwriting credits, encouraging the industry to better acknowledge creators and possibly change how royalties are distributed.
